evidence_set: Oral cancer, snus: four studies from northern Europe found no overall association (Lewin 1998, Schildt 1998, Boffetta 2005, Rosenquist 2005); one Swedish case-control study found no raised risk with either fermented or non-fermented snuff; the Swedish cohort of 9,860 men found RR 3.1 (1.5–6.6) for ever daily use against never daily use of snus and 2.3 (0.7–8.3) in people who never smoked; a cohort of 280,000 construction workers gave 0.8 (0.4–1.7) in men who did not smoke; the Norwegian cohort 1.1 (0.5–2.4) for oral, pharynx or salivary gland cancer. Meta-analyses: northern Europe 1.0 (0.7–1.3) (Boffetta 2008); Scandinavian snuff in people who never smoked 1.01 (0.71–1.45) in 4 studies (Lee and Hamling 2009). The Working Group nonetheless concludes strong evidence that smokeless tobacco as a class causes cancer of the oral cavity.

Oesophagus: Swedish construction-worker cohort, squamous cell carcinoma RR 3.5 (1.6–7.6) in men who did not smoke and used snuff only, against people who never used tobacco; Norwegian cohort 1.4 (0.6–3.2) for ever use of snuff against never use; two Swedish case-control studies OR 1.4 (0.9–2.3, squamous) and 1.2 (0.7–2.0, adenocarcinoma) for users of smokeless tobacco only against non-users of tobacco, and 1.2 (0.7–2.2) for ever use of snuff; of four northern European studies all estimates were above 1.0 but only the Swedish cohort's was significant; meta-analysis of five studies from Europe and the USA 1.6 (1.1–2.3).

Stomach: Swedish cohort of 343,822 men followed 33 years, significant excess of non-cardia stomach cancer among men aged 70 and over who used snus and did not smoke, against never users of any tobacco product, not adjusted for alcohol; other studies not significant, apart from one Indian case-control study of chewing tobacco alone and tuibur; the Working Group did not consider the evidence strong enough to conclude causation. Lung: no significant association in Swedish men who never smoked.

evidence_set: Labelling: of the 44 nicotine-containing products, 15 printed the nicotine content in milligrams per pouch or per gram; 38 used a score or a word for strength; 4 gave no indication of nicotine content at all (no milligram figure, score or word); all but 3 carried a warning for people under 18 and 10 a warning against use in pregnancy. The authors say the contents behind the scores are neither explained nor harmonised. Counted from Table 1 by the AI reader: where a milligram figure with a unit was printed (12 products), measured content was at or below it in 11, with one product 18% above.

Funded by Swedish Match AB, which markets the ZYN and General products described; the funding statement says the funder designed the study, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript, and that analyses and data collection were mainly done at external laboratories where possible. All four authors are affiliated with the company (Regulatory & Scientific Affairs, Stockholm); the competing-interests statement says all authors are either employees of or otherwise funded by it. Seven oral products were screened for 43 compounds, one batch each, triplicate analyses on the whole product, results per gram of wet weight; the two ZYN variants and the snus came from the maker's distribution centre. Most analyses were at an external laboratory accredited to ISO 17025, some in the maker's laboratory; replacement-product methods validated but not accredited.

Nitrosamines: none of ten above the quantification limit in either ZYN variant or either replacement product (limits 0.01 microgram per gram for NNN, NNK, NAT and NAB, roughly 4 to 8 ng per ZYN pouch by the AI reader's arithmetic from Table 1 masses). Snus held NNN 0.44 and NNK 0.19 microgram per gram; loose moist snuff 3.63 and 2.27; pouched moist snuff 2.53 and 0.92, five to 12 times the snus. Below the limit does not mean absent. The independent German laboratory above reports a quantification limit of about 0.4 ng per pouch for NNN (0.7 for NAT, 1.1 for NAB), which is roughly 10 to 20 times lower than the 4 to 8 ng.

Authors' reading: few constituents at low levels in ZYN, suggesting low toxicity; the data are limited to constituent content, and long-term epidemiological data are needed for a full risk assessment. The Background states that long-term epidemiological studies have convincingly shown snus use to be associated with substantially fewer and/or less severe adverse health effects than cigarette smoking (citing one review, which is supported by the same company, see the snus claim) and that tobacco-free pouches should, at least in theory, not expose people to nitrosamines. Only two variants of one brand were tested, one batch each, and no toxicity, uptake or health outcome was measured.

Scope: 481 titles and abstracts screened, 181 full texts, 73 new studies (12 industry-funded), 135 across both reviews; six sources searched to 30 September 2025; English and German; no risk-of-bias assessment and no statistical synthesis; findings are split by industry and non-industry funding. Funding as printed: grant 2U54CA229974 from the US National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute, and the Food and Drug Administration; the funders had no input on the protocol, interpretation or publication. Conflicts as printed: one author received a research grant from Pfizer, served on a scientific advisory board to Johnson & Johnson and consulted for Kenvue outside this work, has consulted for the US Food and Drug Administration, the World Health Organization, the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids and the Polish Medical Research Agency, and is a member of the AACR Tobacco Product and Cancer Subcommittee; another has consulted for Truth Initiative. No tobacco-industry funding or tie is declared.

Who reports use: among adolescents and adults, higher odds of lifetime or current pouch use in males and in people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; older ages among adolescents but younger ages among adults (18 to 25 up to 18 to 64, by study); in US surveys also non-Hispanic whites; education mixed; household income not associated (one US study: income of $75 000 or more linked to higher use). Cross-sectional associations.

Nielsen data (excluding online and specialty shops) show US pouch sales rising from 327 million units in July 2021 to 1,046 million in May 2024 and revenue from US$61 million to US$232 million, with four brands holding 99.8%; exposure to marketing was associated with use and appeal in youth and adults (for youth, exposure to tobacco-product ads in general; one Australian study found no association with susceptibility).

Measured content: a US analysis of 70 oral tobacco-free nicotine products (pouches, loose leaf, toothpicks, lozenges, gum) found 1.41 to 8.11 mg total nicotine per pouch in the pouches, the highest per product; a second analysis of 50 pouches found 6.4 ± 3.5 mg against 12.3 ± 8.2 mg in tobacco-based pouches, with a higher free-base share (63.4% against 47.2%); 31 pouches sold in Germany held 2.20 to 56 mg; measured nicotine was generally equal to or below the label. Elemental analysis of six pouches found aluminium, barium, calcium, chromium, copper, iron, manganese, sodium, scandium, strontium and titanium (presence, not quantified); artificial sweeteners were present at 0.3 to 1.2 mg per pouch, even in those marketed as unflavoured. The paragraph does not label the funders of these content analyses.

Nicotine uptake: in a non-industry-funded five-arm randomized study of pouches sold in Germany, in adults who smoked daily, a 30 mg pouch gave the highest peak and total nicotine over 4 hours, then a cigarette, then 20 mg and 6 mg pouches (time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); in adults who used smokeless tobacco daily, 8 mg pouches delivered comparable or more nicotine than smokeless tobacco after 30 minutes of use; in industry-funded series, 4 mg and 8 mg pouches gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette and 12 mg and 8 mg mini-size pouches comparable or higher, with time to peak 35 to 40 minutes against 5 to 7 for a cigarette; in adults who used Swedish snus (a study the review lists under industry-funded here, but under non-industry-funded in its ratings section), peak and 60-minute nicotine from 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches were higher than from 11.2 mg snus (twice as high for the 11.2 mg pouch), and pouches delivered nicotine slightly faster than snus and nicotine gum. Four of eight new pharmacokinetic trials were industry-funded (British American Tobacco, Japan Tobacco International). The abstract says uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes, which the 6 mg result in this section does not show; the Discussion gives 6 mg or more for the earlier review's studies and 8 mg or more for this update.

Pouches and other nicotine use: in an 8-week three-arm trial of 33 daily smokers of low socioeconomic status with no intention to quit, those assigned to pouches cut cigarettes per day by nearly half from the baseline average of 15, one person switched completely and three stopped using pouches; in a 4-week trial of 30, both 3 mg and 6 mg strengths cut cigarettes and two people on 6 mg stopped smoking; in a 6-month industry-funded trial of 100 with a continued-smoking control group, cigarettes per day in the pouch group fell by over 90% from baseline; in a US cross-sectional study, quitting cigarettes was associated with daily pouch use; 73% of Pakistani adults currently using pouches also smoked; 41% of Saudi adults with a tobacco history who tried pouches reported quitting smoking with them (38% reported cutting down). (Whether pouches help people stop smoking is a separate claim.)

Biomarkers and physiology in people: in PATH data (small sample), nicotine metabolites in people who used only pouches were higher than in people who used only e-cigarettes and comparable to people who smoked; minor tobacco alkaloids, cadmium and uranium were lower than in people who smoked and similar to people who vape; lead was lower than in people who smoked or vaped; in the 4-week trial, dual use with pouches did not lower tobacco-specific nitrosamines; 20-minute use of 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette (the non-industry-funded five-arm study of pouches sold in Germany); an Altria-funded trial found less gingivitis and enamel staining at 24 weeks in adults who smoked daily and switched to pouches, compared with those who continued smoking.

Pouch evidence base (15 studies): five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (blood pressure, heart rate, craving, abuse potential; one 9-hour trial funded by the manufacturer), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional symptom surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214, 831) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272). The longest follow-up stated is 6 months (none is given for the national cohort); no study follows disease or death. Counts of designs are the editors' reading of Table 1. Search to 25 July 2026, English only; funded by the Medical University of Lodz; no competing interests declared; the review does not report who funded most included studies.

Pouch symptoms in Saudi Arabian surveys, reported in the review as prevalences among people who use pouches: bloating 66.7%, nausea 47.9%, heartburn 46.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%, frequent cough or wheeze 27.8%, any psychological effect 39.3%, taste or smell change 36.7%, dry mouth 39.8%. The review gives no estimate of what share of a comparable group without pouches would report the same symptoms.

Pouch oral findings: among 272 young Swedish adults, oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% in people who use pouches (n = 126) against 89% and 79% in people who use snus (n = 63); the review reports erythema (44% against 32% in snus), oedema (15%), etch damage (8%) and mucosal ulcers (2%) as higher in the pouch group than in the snus group, and gingival recession as lower (45% against 52%). After 23 dentists switched from snus to pouches, snus lesion severity fell from 95.7% to 69.6% and gingival irritation from 43.5% to 4.3%. In a randomized trial of adults who smoked (n printed as 155), gingival and bleeding indices were 20% to 30% lower at 12 and 24 weeks after switching to pouches, compared with continued smoking and baseline (the review does not separate the two); Kopa-Stojak gives no funder, but Travis 2026 names the matching trial (Liu 2025) as Altria-funded.
